first.rationale: With only one experiment slot, the competitor's aggressive pricing creates pressure toward promotional_pricing, but memory_73 explicitly flags that this tactic drives strong acquisition/revenue lift while materially harming 30-day retention—directly conflicting with the objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue. Verifying memory_73's archived record confirms whether that retention harm was robust and not context-specific before ruling it out. Meanwhile, onboarding completion is down 4% QoQ and memory_31/memory_86 show durable, non-conflicting evidence that signup/onboarding simplification lifts activation and time-to-value without noted downside—directly addressing both the activation and onboarding declines simultaneously. Verifying memory_31's source confirms the durability claim before committing scarce capacity. Referral incentives and activation messaging are viable but address only one symptom each and are lower urgency than the compounding onboarding/activation problem. Enterprise sales-assist is unrelated to the SMB-side declines and competitive threat. I'm treating this as a standard experiment rather than broad rollout since QoQ declines warrant a fresh, moderately-scaled test to reconfirm the effect still holds under current competitive conditions rather than assuming full transfer of an older result.

final.rationale: Verification confirms exp_73: promotional pricing produces a 12% retention hit and a cohort that doesn't survive first renewal—directly contradicts the sustainable long-term qualified revenue objective, so it's ruled out despite competitive pressure to match the competitor's pricing move. Verification also confirms exp_31: signup simplification on SMB delivered +9% activation with only -1% retention and +4% qualified revenue, a durable and low-risk result, though it's confirmed specifically for SMB and not replicated on other segments. This aligns well with two of the three current problems (activation down 6% QoQ, onboarding completion down 4% QoQ) and complements memory_86's finding that shortened onboarding lifts completion and time-to-value. Referral incentives (memory_57) and activation messaging (memory_91) are reasonable alternatives but address only one symptom each and lack the same direct confirmation just obtained. Enterprise sales-assist doesn't address the SMB-side declines or competitive pressure. Given only one experiment slot this week, simplify_onboarding is the best-supported, lowest-risk choice that targets the compounding activation/onboarding problem without the retention harm seen in the pricing route. Scaling as a standard experiment (not broad rollout) respects that this is a fresh run under current conditions and that exp_31 was SMB-specific, not universally replicated.
